title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 373
paragraphs: Psammetichos' son was Necos, and he became king of Egypt. He was the first to attempt the canal connecting the Nile to the Red Sea, which Darius the Persian later completed. The canal is a four-day voyage in length and wide enough for two triremes to be rowed side by side. The water comes from the Nile. The canal runs from a point slightly above the city of Bubastis, past the Arabian city of Patumos, and into the Red Sea. The first part runs along the Arabian side of the Egyptian plain, past the ridge that extends south of Memphis, where the stone quarries are. The canal follows the base of this ridge from west to east, then turns south through a gap in the hills toward the Arabian Gulf. The shortest and most direct route from the northern sea to the southern (or Red) Sea is across the strip from Mount Casion on the border of Egypt and Syria—a distance of exactly a thousand furlongs. That is the most direct route. The canal is much longer because it winds. A hundred and twenty thousand Egyptians died during the digging under Necos. He eventually stopped because an oracle warned him he was working for the benefit of a barbarian. (The Egyptians call anyone who does not speak their language a barbarian.)
